The word turnout has several distinct meanings. I'll walk you through each one clearly, with examples, so you understand exactly when and how each is used.
Meaning 1: The number of people who attend or participate in something

This is the most common and widely used meaning in modern English.

When someone says "turnout," they usually mean how many people showed up — to a vote, a protest, a concert, a match, a meeting, or any public event. It measures attendance or participation.

Examples:

  • "Voter turnout was very low in this election." → Fewer people than expected actually came out to vote.
  • "Despite heavy rain, there was a great turnout at the charity run." → Many people still showed up.
  • "The festival attracted a record turnout of 80,000 people." → 80,000 people attended.

Notice that turnout isn't just a raw number — it often carries a sense of how impressive or disappointing the attendance was. A "high turnout" is good; a "low turnout" is concerning.

You will very frequently see it paired with:

  • voter turnout — the proportion of eligible voters who actually voted
  • high/low turnout
  • strong/poor turnout
  • record turnout — more people than ever before
Meaning 2: A widened section of a narrow road

On narrow roads — especially rural or mountain roads — where two vehicles cannot pass each other side by side, builders construct occasional wider spots at intervals along the road. One vehicle can pull into this wider section and wait while the other passes. That wider section is called a turnout.

It is also used for a small area beside a main road where a driver can pull over temporarily — to check a map, take a photo, rest, or let emergency vehicles pass.

Examples:

  • "The mountain road was barely one lane wide, but every kilometer there was a turnout where cars could let each other pass."
  • "The driver pulled into a turnout and switched off the engine."

This meaning is especially common in American English and in contexts involving rural or scenic roads.
Meaning 3: A railway switch or junction

In railway terminology, a turnout is the mechanical arrangement of tracks that allows a train to move from one track onto another branching track. It is the point where one line diverges from another.

In British English, this same thing is often called "points"; in American English, it is called a "switch" or a "turnout."

Example:

  • "The train slowed as it approached the turnout to shift onto the branch line."
Meaning 4: A person's appearance, outfit, or a smart horse-drawn carriage (old-fashioned / literary)

In older or more formal English — the kind you find in 19th- and early 20th-century literature — turnout referred to the overall way a person was dressed and presented, their smartness of appearance. It could also refer to a complete horse-drawn carriage along with its horses, harness, and driver — the whole package as a visual display.

Examples:

  • "The general's turnout was flawless — uniform pressed, buttons gleaming, posture perfect." → His appearance and presentation were immaculate.
  • "The duchess arrived in an admirable turnout." → She arrived in a fine, well-equipped carriage with matched horses.

You will mostly encounter this meaning in classic literature or period dramas. It is rarely used in everyday modern speech, but knowing it will help you understand older texts.
Meaning 5: A thorough clearing-out or cleaning of a space (chiefly British English)

In British English, a turnout can mean the act of emptying a room, cupboard, drawer, or storage space — going through everything, sorting it out, throwing away what is no longer needed, and cleaning the space.

Examples:

  • "I gave the spare room a good turnout and donated three boxes of old books."
  • "The office is overdue for a turnout — there are files here from fifteen years ago."

You will hear this mostly in informal British speech.
Meaning 6: A workers' strike or walkout (historical)

In 19th-century British English — particularly in writing about the Industrial Revolution and factory labour — a turnout meant a strike, where workers collectively stopped working and "turned out" of the factory in protest to demand better pay or conditions.

Example:

  • "The mill workers organized a turnout to protest the wage cuts."

This meaning is now obsolete in everyday use, but you will come across it in historical texts, novels, and accounts from that era.
How to tell which meaning is intended

Since turnout carries several meanings, context always makes it clear:

  • Talking about an election, rally, concert, or gathering? → It means the number of people who attended.
  • Talking about a road? → It means a wider section where vehicles can pull over.
  • Talking about a railway? → It means a track switch or junction.
  • Talking about someone's appearance or a carriage? → It means their outfit/presentation or the whole vehicle.
  • Talking about cleaning a room or storage? → It means a clearout (British).
  • In a historical, industrial context about workers? → It means a strike.
A note on the word's feel

The word turnout always carries a sense of something coming outward or into view. People turn out (come out) for an event. A road turns out (broadens outward). A railway turns out (branches outward). A person's appearance is what they turn out to the world. Workers turn out of a factory. This shared sense of emerging or spreading outward is woven through every meaning.
